6._section_summary: This section describes a 5-item face-valid daily measure created to assess frequency of interactions with body-focused and non-body-focused others. Factor analyses revealed two factors (Exposure to Body-Focused Others and Exposure to Non-Body Focused Others) with item loadings and acceptable Cronbach's alpha ranges across days; mean weekly frequencies were reported (non-body focused = 2.97, SD = 0.87; body focused = 2.00, SD = 0.83). No explicit study labeling (e.g., 'Study 1') or participant/sample demographics (N, age, country, BMI, race/ethnicity, recruitment method) are provided in this section.

It explains creation of between-person (person means) and two kinds of within-person predictors (daily deviations from person mean and day-to-day difference/lag variables), and two sets of multilevel models: one examining within-day and across-week effects (with BMI and mean exposures as level-2 covariates) and one examining day-to-day changes (with lagged criterion variables and BMI as covariate). The section does not label any study as 'Study 1' or report sample demographics or measurement instruments.

10._section_summary: This section reports intraclass correlations (ICCs) and within- and between-person correlations for the study variables, noting ICCs for exposure to body-focused and non-body-focused others (.50 and .44) and for body appreciation (.77). Within-person correlations were generally null for relations between exposures and criteria, whereas between-persons analyses showed that higher mean exposure to non-body-focused others related to higher intuitive eating, and higher mean exposure to body-focused others related to lower intuitive eating and body appreciation (p < .10) and higher dietary restraint. The section references Table 1 for detailed correlations and does not label multiple studies (no 'Study 1' or similar).

13._section_summary: The section reports multilevel model results linking exposure to non-body focused and body focused others with intuitive eating: between-persons, higher average exposure to non-body focused others predicted greater intuitive eating and higher average exposure to body focused others predicted lower intuitive eating. Within-persons analyses showed trends and lagged effects such that day-to-day increases in exposure to non-body focused others predicted greater intuitive eating, and changes in intuitive eating predicted subsequent exposure to non-body focused others. Table 2 (and Table 3 referenced) present the reported betas and model details.

14.evidence_source: As shown in Table 2, at the between-persons level, mean exposure to non-body focused others (Hypothesis 1a) negatively predicted dietary restraint at a trend level, and mean exposure to body focused others (Hypothesis 2b) was a significant positive predictor of restraint.
14._section_summary: This section reports within- and between-persons multilevel results relating exposure to body-focused and non-body-focused others to dietary restraint and other body-image and eating outcomes. Between-persons, greater typical exposure to body-focused others predicted more dietary restraint and greater exposure to non-body-focused others predicted less restraint; within-persons, day-to-day increases in exposure to non-body-focused others predicted less dietary restraint but exposure to body-focused others did not predict same-day or next-day outcomes. The section does not label multiple studies or experiments explicitly.
